title: Pearl purl couching
subtitle: A springy beaded metal coil couched into its own twists to create a raised metallic outline
excerpt: Pearl purl is a coiled metal thread whose loops give it a beaded appearance. It is laid along a line without stretching and couched by stitching a fine thread into the grooves between each loop, so the couching thread disappears and only the metal shows. The result is a crisp, raised outline with a rope-like texture.
sourceNotes: Barbara Dawson, Metal Thread Embroidery (1968), pearl purl chapter. Royal School of Needlework standard goldwork curriculum. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), purl outline entries.

glossaryTerms.definition: A springy coiled metal wire with a beaded or pearl-like appearance. Unlike smooth purl, it is not cut into chips; it is used in continuous lengths and couched into its own loops.

content.text: Pearl purl gives a goldwork design the look of a fine metal rope drawn around each shape. It is a springy coiled wire: the loops of the coil create the beaded surface texture, and those same loops act as ready-made channels for the couching thread. Because the binding stitches sink between the loops rather than lying across the thread,
looks entirely metallic when finished. It is never stretched before couching; keeping it relaxed preserves the bead texture.

items.label: Metal thread
items.value: Pearl purl, size 1 or 2; cut with small sharp scissors, not pulled apart

items.label: Couching thread
items.value: One strand of waxed yellow silk or fine gold thread; wax with beeswax before stitching

items.label: Ground
items.value: Firm silk or linen, mounted tightly on a slate frame; felt padding or string padding beneath the outline area raises the pearl purl further

items.label: Needle
items.value: Fine sharps needle size 10, small enough to pass between the coil loops without forcing them apart

content.text: Measure the length of the outline to be covered and cut a length of pearl purl to match. Cut cleanly between two loops using small sharp scissors; never pull the coil apart as this distorts the beads.
Position the pearl purl along the drawn line. Thread the fine needle with a single strand of waxed silk. Bring the needle up on one side of the purl at the start of the line.

Pass the needle across the pearl purl and down into the fabric on the other side, catching the thread between two loops of the coil. The stitch sinks into a groove rather than lying over the top of the metal. Pull the thread through so the stitch disappears between the loops.

Continue couching every two or three loops along the entire length. On a curve, couch every loop to hold the purl to the line without pulling it out of shape. Do not stretch the purl; let it sit naturally with its loops intact.

At the end, make a final couching stitch through the last loop. Trim any excess cleanly. The cut ends do not need to be plunged as with passing thread; a secure couching stitch at each end holds them.

attrs.heading: When pearl purl couching goes wrong

items.symptom: The beaded texture flattens and the outline looks like a plain wire
items.cause: The pearl purl was stretched before or during couching.
items.fix: Work with the purl in its relaxed state. Lay it on the line and couch it as it naturally sits. Tension on the couching stitch should only be enough to secure it, not to compress the loops.

items.symptom: The couching thread is visible across the surface of the purl
items.cause: The needle passed over the coil instead of between the loops.
items.fix: Use the finest needle that will carry the thread and guide it deliberately into a groove between two loops. The thread must sink between the loops, not sit on top.

items.symptom: The purl will not follow a tight curve and lifts away from the line
items.cause: Too few couching stitches on the curve, or the purl is too large a size for the radius.
items.fix: Increase couching to every loop on curves. On very tight curves, use a smaller purl size such as size 0, which has smaller loops and more flexibility.
